name: Optery
tagline: Record discovered public-profile pages and guide the user through legitimate opt-outs

tiers.name: Basic
tiers.limits: Exposure report and screenshots; self-service opt-out tools; report refresh roughly quarterly after recent login

tiers.name: Core
tiers.limits: Automated removals from 150+ sites, or 380+ with Expanded Reach; 1 name and 1 city/state variant; monthly scans

tiers.name: Extended
tiers.limits: Automated removals from 325+ sites, or 555+ with Expanded Reach; unlimited name/address variants; human-agent support
tiers.notes: $149 billed annually; reports roughly every 90 days.

tiers.name: Ultimate
tiers.limits: Automated removals from 405+ sites, or 635+ with Expanded Reach; unlimited custom removals for 950+ eligible sites after 30 days

pricing.freeTierCaps: Exposure report/screenshots and self-service opt-out instructions; no automated removals
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; no free trial; 30-day money-back guarantee
pricing.hiddenCosts: Core/Extended/Ultimate coverage differs materially by site count; family groups receive 20% off for 2 paid members, 25% for 3 and 30% for 4+, while upgrades are prorated and use the same billing term

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Optery, record discovered public-profile pages and guide the user through legitimate opt-outs. The hard boundary is proprietary scanning coverage, screenshots, automated removals, human review, and monitoring, plus security assurance, infrastructure, and trust.
coreLoopDIY: Record discovered public-profile pages, guide the user through legitimate opt-outs, store tracking data locally with strong encryption, and make no claim of replacing an audited removal service.
whatYouLose: proprietary scanning coverage, screenshots, automated removals, human review, and monitoring
ongoingBurden: cryptography, secure updates, key recovery, threat intelligence, relay capacity, abuse response, audits, and incident handling
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Optery because security products are paid for because expert review, infrastructure, and accountability matter more than recreating screens. The recurring cost buys cryptography, secure updates, key recovery, threat intelligence, relay capacity, abuse response, audits, and incident handling, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Vaultwarden
priorArt.desc: Widely used Bitwarden-compatible self-hosted password server implementation.

alternatives.name: California DROP
alternatives.desc: California residents get one government request to 600-plus brokers; everyone else gets a geography lesson.

facts.install: Government-hosted browser signup followed by one deletion request
facts.dataFormat: Personal identifiers encrypted before storage in CalPrivacy's DROP system and matched by registered data brokers
facts.gapVsPaid: It covers only eligible California residents and registered brokers, without Optery's discovery screenshots and individualized exposure tracking.
facts.setupBlocker: Only California residents are eligible, and the request requires personal identifiers for broker matching

alternatives.name: Optery Free Basic
alternatives.desc: Finds the profiles and hands you the opt-out links; your unpaid labor is the business model.

facts.install: Hosted signup followed by identity and profile intake
facts.dataFormat: Personal profile data, exposure findings and screenshots in Optery's AWS-hosted cloud account, encrypted in transit and at rest
facts.gapVsPaid: The free tier scans periodically and provides self-service links but does not run Optery's automated removals.
facts.setupBlocker: Providing enough sensitive identity and address history for accurate broker matching

alternatives.name: Permission Slip by DeleteMe
alternatives.desc: A phone app that sends individual privacy requests and tracks them; bulk broker removal is the paid part.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Mozilla Monitor
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Everyone still links it; Mozilla shut the broker-removal product down and deleted its scan data.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Extended plan and a educational or low-risk personal utility DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Optery in an empty repository.
Use Rust, Tauri 2, React, SQLite, Argon2id, and audited cryptographic libraries; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: record discovered public-profile pages, guide the user through legitimate opt-outs, store tracking data locally with strong encryption, and make no claim of replacing an audited removal service.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Write a plain-language threat model before implementing any sensitive feature.
Keep all vault data encrypted with a master key derived through Argon2id and a unique salt.
Use authenticated encryption from a maintained library and never invent cryptographic primitives.
Implement lock timeout, clipboard clearing, password generation, import, export, and encrypted backups.
Make recovery-key creation explicit and test restore from a fresh installation.
Display a persistent warning that the build has not received an independent security audit.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out a production VPN or anonymity network.
Deliberately leave out identity-protection monitoring and data-broker removal.
Deliberately leave out enterprise security guarantees, audits, and emergency support.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
